summary: This informational document evaluates existing IETF routing protocols against the routing requirements of an Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON) as defined by ITU-T. It builds on the Generalized MPLS suite, which controls technologies such as SONET/SDH and optical transport networks.

eli5.summary: A company wants to know whether existing road maps work for a new kind of light-based highway. This document checks them against the list of things the highway needs.

questions: can ospf and is-is support gmpls ason
why is bgp not used for ason routing
what is the is-is up down bit
subtitle: A checklist of how well OSPF and IS-IS can carry the routing needs of ITU-T optical networks, and what they would need added.

tldr.problem: ITU-T defines routing requirements for an Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON), and RFC 4258 restates them for GMPLS. Nobody had checked whether existing IETF routing protocols meet them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC compares OSPF and IS-IS with the requirements one topic at a time: identification, link and node attributes, reachability, hierarchy, convergence and scoping. It sets BGP aside as a candidate.
tldr.outcome: Most requirements are already met. A short list of additions is needed, mainly prefix reachability, cross-layer link attributes, scoping several logical nodes under one router, and loop prevention between hierarchy levels.

facts.label: IS-IS up/down bit
facts.value: 0 when first injected, 1 once sent down

today: RFC 4652 is an Informational evaluation and, according to the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It reflects the state of the protocols in October 2006 and lists additions that were still needed at the time.

sections.title: Purpose and Candidate Protocols
sections.content:
The ITU-T ASON control plane architecture is defined in G.8080. RFC 4258 gives the routing requirements for the GMPLS routing suite to support ASON, but it does not address whether GMPLS routing protocols can meet them. This document makes that evaluation, with results in Section 5 and the evaluation scenarios in Section 6.

The candidates are the interior gateway protocols, OSPF and IS-IS. BGP is not addressed, mainly for three reasons: it does not exchange traffic engineering information, it only advertises its one best route per prefix so routers know little about topology, and it is not widely deployed in optical equipment and networks.
sections.eli5: There was a list of what the new highway needs. This document asks whether the old maps, called OSPF and IS-IS, can already do it.

sections.title: What ASON Asks of Routing
sections.content:
The routing protocol must support Routing Areas (RAs) with unique identifiers inside a carrier's network, and carry hierarchical routing information, including summarized information for other levels. The number of hierarchy levels is implementation specific. It must use a common set of information elements for links and abstract nodes, and it must converge so that the distributed routing databases (RDBs) end up synchronized.

For hierarchy, it must process information exchanged between adjacent levels, keep it self-consistent after filtering or summarizing, and prevent information from being passed back to the level it came from. A sub-network or RA must be able to present itself to the wider network as a single logical entity with only its external links visible. Using one routing protocol in an RA should not restrict the choice in other RAs.
sections.eli5: The highway needs neighborhoods with their own names, maps that can be zoomed in and out, and every map agreeing in the end. A map must also never send news back to where it came from.

sections.title: Identifiers and Scoping
sections.content:
The RFC uses a few symbols. Pi is a physical node in the data plane. Li is a logical control plane entity tied to one abstract data plane node, identified by the TE Router ID. Ri is a control plane router that originates topology information, identified by its Router_ID, which is a 32-bit ID in OSPF and a 48-bit System ID in IS-IS. Si is a signaling function.

An Li may be advertised by only one Ri at a time, but one Ri may advertise several Lis. So the routing protocol MUST be able to advertise multiple TE Router IDs and MUST be able to tell which TE Router ID each advertised link and each piece of reachability information belongs to. Because unnumbered links have IDs defined per Li, the advertisement must name the remote Lj to scope the link.

The control plane exchanges only its own identifiers. The mapping to transport plane identifiers stays local, for example from 192.0.2.1 to 666B.F999.AF10.222C. The RFC concludes that OSPF and IS-IS carry sufficient node identification, and that GMPLS link state protocols can provide RA identification without change.
sections.eli5: Each building has a street name in the control room and a different serial number on the real machine. Only the street name is shared, and the control room keeps the match private.

sections.title: Link, Node and Reachability Information
sections.content:
Almost every ASON link characteristic already maps to an existing sub-TLV in GMPLS OSPF-TE and IS-IS-TE. Examples are the link weight (TE metric), resource class (Administrative Group), diversity support (SRLG) and link availability (Link Protection). The exception is Local Adaptation support, because GMPLS routing has no dedicated attribute for cross-layer relationships.

Bandwidth needs more thought. GMPLS describes bandwidth per priority through the Interface Switching Capability Descriptor and the Unreserved Bandwidth sub-TLV. ASON could also account in tuples of signal type and number of unallocated timeslots, which may need new signal types. The RFC calls the approach of RFC 4202 the most straightforward, since it needs no change in bandwidth accounting.

Node attributes are the logical node ID plus reachability. A draft can advertise a router's local host addresses in OSPF, but not prefixes, so a prefix length or network mask mechanism is needed. IS-IS has no similar mechanism, and its Extended IP Reachability TLV focuses on IP end-points.
sections.eli5: Most of the facts the highway wants to know, like how long a road is or how risky it is, already have a place on the map. A few, like how layers connect, have no place yet.

sections.title: Hierarchy and Convergence
sections.content:
ASON allows static and dynamic abstraction of routing information, but the result is still ordinary link and node advertisements. Abstraction methods are outside the scope of GMPLS routing, so the protocol only needs to know when information originates outside an RA.

The main problem is loops: if routing controllers at adjacent levels redistribute in both directions, they cannot detect looping information. IS-IS handles this for IP reachability with the up/down bit defined in RFC 2966. It is 0 when information is first injected and set to 1 when it travels down, and information with the bit set may only go further down. That does not cover the Extended IS Reachability TLV (Type 22) used for summarized topology and TE information.

OSPFv2 stops inter-area routes learned from area 0 from returning there, but GMPLS uses Type 10 (area-local) Opaque LSAs for TE information. So those LSAs need a way to show that information was learned from a higher-level controller.

For convergence, link state protocols propagate topology changes with a short convergence period, which the RFC finds sufficient for ASON.
sections.eli5: When news travels between big and small neighborhoods, it needs a sticker that says which way it was going so it never gets sent back and goes around forever.

sections.title: Required Additions and Security
sections.content:
The RFC summarizes what OSPFv2 and IS-IS would need. Both need reachability for prefixes, cross-layer link attribute representation, optionally per-signal-type bandwidth accounting, scoping of links and prefixes to the right TE Router_ID, and a hierarchy loop-prevention mechanism. For OSPF this is a Type 10 Opaque LSA marker. For IS-IS it is extending the up/down bit to summarized topology, TE information and reachability.

On security, a dynamic control plane exposes an ASON to additional risks, since routing protocols can be attacked into instability or into giving wrong information to path computation and signaling. The RFC says there is no reason the control plane cannot be secured and that the security mechanisms developed for Internet routing protocols apply equally.
sections.eli5: The to-do list is short: add a way to describe whole address blocks, a place for layer links, a way to tell which machine owns what, and a sticker to stop news looping. Keep the whole thing locked against tampering.

Cross/inter-layer relationships in the top-level link TLV
Cross/inter-layer relationships in the Extended IS Reachability TLV
